title: Artery of Percheron Infarction: A Case Report of Bilateral Thalamic Stroke Presenting with Acute Encephalopathy
case_prompt: A 56-year-old African American woman with a history of nonischemic cardiomyopathy, hypertension, COPD, hyperlipidemia, left ventricular thrombus on rivaroxaban, depression, anxiety, and polysubstance use disorder was found unresponsive in a house frequented by drug abusers and brought to the emergency department with acute encephalopathy of unknown cause. On admission, her Glasgow Coma Scale was 7, which improved after administration of 2 mg of naloxone. There were no focal neurologic deficits. She intermittently desaturated to 84% with an episode of apnea and was placed on 3–4 L of oxygen via nasal cannula. Her blood pressure was 152/100 mmHg. Laboratory studies showed a sodium level of 133 mEq/L, a creatine kinase level of 1281 U/L, and normal alcohol, salicylate, and acetaminophen levels. A urine drug screen was positive for amphetamines, cocaine, and cannabinoids. Noncontrast head CT revealed hypodensities in both thalami, prompting a teleneurology consultation; thrombolysis was withheld because of rivaroxaban use and unclear timing of symptom onset. CT angiography did not identify any isolated vessel occlusion. Brain MRI with gadolinium demonstrated vivid enhancement in both thalami and the upper midbrain, consistent with subacute infarction. MR venography showed a patent intracranial venous system.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Considered cerebral venous thrombosis — “MR venogram (MRV) demonstrated a patent intracranial venous system (not shown).”  
2. Considered basilar artery thrombosis — “CT angiogram (CTA) did not identify an isolated vessel occlusion.”  
3. Considered metabolic or toxic etiologies — “the bilateral and frequently symmetrical imaging abnormalities in the thalami and midbrain in conjunction with prominent mental status findings often initially point to a metabolic or toxic etiology, delaying the diagnosis of an uncommon stroke syndrome.”
